Short communication
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus preceding otherwise
asymptomatic Hodgkin's lymphoma
Caroline Schmidt a,1, Tobias Freilinger a,⁎,1, M. Lieb b, J. Rémi a, M. Klein a, A. Straube a, T. Pfefferkorn a
a Department of Neurology, Klinikum Großhadern der Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Munich, Germany
b Department of Psychiatry, Ludwig-Maximilians-Universität München, Munich, Germany

Keywords:
Hodgkin's lymphoma
Stiff-person syndrome
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity
and myoclonus
PERM
Paraneoplastic
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS), a rare neuroimmunological disorder, is characterized by symmetrical rigidity
and muscle stiffness, particularly of axial and proximal limb muscles. Progressive encephalomyelitis with
rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) is a variant of SPS which includes additional clinical features (e.g. sensory
symptoms, brain stem signs and pathological CSF ﬁndings). An association of both SPS and PERM with (solid)
malignancies has been previously reported. Beyond this, there have been single reports of SPS in the setting
of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL). Here, we present a case of PERM associated with HL, with PERM preceding
occurrence of lymphoma by more than seven months. Our observation has obvious implications for the
management and, in particular, diagnostic evaluation of patients with PERM.

1. Introduction
Stiff-person syndrome (SPS) is a rare neuroimmunological disorder
characterized by symmetrical rigidity and muscle stiffness, particularly
of axial and proximal limb muscles [1–3]. Spasms of increased rigidity,
sometimes accompanied by intense pain, can be superimposed, either
spontaneously or elicited by external sensory stimuli. Other features
include autonomic symptoms, exaggerated startle responses, epileptic
seizures and paroxysmal fear. The pathophysiology is not understood
completely, but preliminary evidence has suggested a role of immune-
mediated processes. Antibodies against glutamic acid decarboxylase
(antiGADAb) are detected in up to 80% of patients; however their
pathophysiological signiﬁcance has not yet been ﬁrmly established.
Progressive encephalomyelitis with rigidity and myoclonus (PERM) is a
variant of SPS with additional features such as sensory symptoms, brain
stem signs and pathological CSF ﬁndings [2].
Previous authors have reported an association of SPS and PERM with
malignancies, in particular solid tumors such as breast and small cell
lung cancer [2], but also hematological malignancies[4]. Three previous
reports have described SPS in the context of Hodgkin's lymphoma (HL)
[5–7]. Here, we present a case of PERM associated with HL, with PERM
preceding clinically asymptomatic occurrence of lymphoma by more
than seven months.
2. Case report
The patient is a 21-year-old Caucasian man. Past medical history was
remarkable for abuse of cannabis for the past 18 months and a self-
reported episode of depression. Initially, he was admitted to a
psychiatric hospital because of generalized pruritus, paroxysmal fear
and disturbance of sleep. Apart from drug screening, which was positive
for tetrahydrocannabinol, initial work-up including CSF analysis was
normal. Within a few days, he developed rapidly progressive gait ataxia,

postural instability and generalized myoclonic jerks, leading to frequent
falls, complicated by jaw and right clavicle fracture which caused
traumatic mediastinal emphysema. Because of increasing autonomic
symptoms and respiratory distress requiring intubation and mechanic
ventilation, the patient was transferred to the local intensive care unit
(ICU). Two days later, a generalized tonic–clonic seizure occurred, and
IV phenytoin was initiated. A second spinal tap revealed mild
pleocytosis (18 white blood cells/µl; differentiation not available);
protein (35 mg/dl) and glucose (96 mg/dl) were unremarkable.
Calculated antiviral therapy with acyclovir was started, and the patient
was transferred to our neurological ICU.
After analgesia and sedation were tapered off, neurological
examination showed a minimally responsive patient with bilateral
ptosis and mydriasis, hypometric saccades and generalized myoclonic
jerks, occurring spontaneously and after triggering by external
sensory stimuli. Muscle tone was severely increased, and Babinski

sign was bilaterally positive. The patient followed simple commands,
but did not make any attempt to explore his surroundings actively.
Although he was awake and had no muscular weakness, mechanical
ventilation was necessary because of reduced spontaneous breathing
and increased CO 2 retention; extubation was not possible.
Blood chemistry, hematology, liver function tests, coagulation studies
and vasculitis parameters (C3, C4, rheumatoid factor, anti-nuclear
antibodies, double-stranded DNA-antibodies, anti-cytoplasmatic anti-
bodies) were all within normal limits. In particular, antibodies against
GAD (determined by radioimmunoassay), amphiphysin (determined by
immunoblot), acetylcholine receptors, muscle-speciﬁc tyrosine kinase
(MuSK), titin, and voltage-gated calcium channels as well as antineur-
onal antibodies (anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Ma 2, anti-CV2) were all negative.
Another CSF analysis was performed, which revealed normal results for
cells (<1/µl), total protein (20 mg/dl) and glucose (81 mg/dl); the CSF/
serum ratios for both albumin and IgG were within the reference range,
and oligoclonal bands were not detected. Microbiological analysis of CSF
samples was unremarkable. The further clinical course was complicated
by recurring episodes of severe autonomic crises, including tachyar-
rhythmia, hyperthermia, hyperhidrosis, hypersalivation and paralytic
ileus. Repeated cranial and spinal magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)
with and without contrast was unremarkable, without evidence of
encephalitic lesions. EEG ruled out status epilepticus, and extra- and
intracranial Doppler- and duplexsonography were normal. Nerve
conduction studies and EMG of extremity muscles were unremarkable,
without signs of neuropathy or myopathy. By contrast, EMG of axial
muscles revealed continuous motor unit activity, which could be
increased by tactile stimulation of other parts of the body. Based on
this, a working diagnosis of stiff-person syndrome/PERM was made, and
empiric therapy with benzodiazepines (3 mg lorazepam 6×/day) and
high-dose IV methylprednisolone (5× 500 mg) was started[8],l e a d i n g
to substantial clinical improvement.
Bone-marrow biopsy was unremarkable. At that time, whole-body
computed tomography (CT) and 18F-FDG positron emission tomog-
raphy (PET) did not show any pathological lesions except for
minimally increased glucose metabolism in a few infracarinal/hilar
lymph nodes ( Fig. 1a), compatible with in ﬂammatory changes in the
context of aspiration pneumonia which the patient suffered from
during ICU treatment. Histological examination of endobroncheal
lavage as well as transbroncheal lymph node biopsies showed only
signs of in ﬂammation, but was without evidence of malignancy.
Two months after admission the patient was discharged to a
neuro-rehabilitation centre with oral steroids (40 mg methylprednis-
olone qd), IV benzodiazepines (3 mg lorazepam 6×/day) and oral
tiagabine (5 mg qd). He was fed orally and could stand and walk with
only minimal assistance.
Seven months after initial presentation the patient returned for an
elective follow-up evaluation. The medication with oral corticoids had
been tapered off in the meantime, and lorazepam had been reduced to
1.25 mg po tid. His status had signi ﬁcantly improved: He reported
cramps of the abdominal muscles which occurred sporadically when
in a supine position, but was otherwise without complaints. On
neurological examination there was persistent bilateral mild ptosis

and bilaterally positive Babinski sign, but no other abnormal ﬁndings.
EMG of axial muscles did not show any pathological spontaneous
activity. However, PET-CT revealed increased metabolism in several
enlarged mediastinal as well as left-sided supraclavicular lymph
nodes ( Fig. 1 b, c, d). Histological and immunohistochemical evalua-
tion of bioptic specimens established a diagnosis of nodular sclerosing
HL. A total of four cycles of polychemotherapy were performed

enlarged mediastinal lymph nodes which show pathologically increased PET activity (c). d. The panel shows an overlay of (b) and (c).

according to the ABVD protocol (doxorubicin, bleomycin, vinblastine,
and dacarbazine). Follow-up PET-CT four months after the ﬁrst cycle
revealed a signi ﬁcant reduction of the previously enlarged and
hypermetabolic lymph nodes, indicating a good treatment response.
Another two months later, no pathological PET activity was
detectable. During chemotherapy, the neurological status of the
patient showed progressive further improvement. There were no
more cramps of axial muscles or startle responses, the pruritus
subsided and the medication with benzodiazepines and tiagabine
could be tapered off completely. The patient was able to return to
school and had no limitations in his daily life. Fourteen months after
diagnosis of HL he returned to the hospital for a follow-up evaluation
which showed a normal neurological examination, with only minimal
residual bilateral ptosis.
3. Discussion
The most likely diagnosis which explains all the systemic and
neurological symptoms of our patient is PERM. All other differential
diagnoses can explain only a subset of signs and symptoms. For
example, the bilateral ptosis would be compatible with a diagnosis of
ocular myasthenia, but other symptoms and antibodies against AcChR
were absent, and there was no pathological decrement upon serial
stimulation of cranial muscles. The pathological CSFﬁndings could have
suggested encephalitis, but imaging studies and microbiological
investigations were all negative. Considering the previous history of
drug abuse and the severe autonomic features, a diagnosis of drug
withdrawal could have been considered, but this would not account for
the brain stem signs, the pathological CSFﬁndings and the electrophys-
iological abnormalities. Likewise, a primarily psychiatric diagnosis, e.g.
catatonic stupor, would only explain some of the behavioural
abnormalities, but is not compatible with most of the neurological
symptoms, in particular the reduced spontaneous breathing. Some
aspects of the clinical presentation of our patient, including the
psychiatric abnormalities as well as the profound autonomic dysfunc-
tion, are similar to what has been described for anti-NMDA-receptor
encephalitis [9]. Testing for anti-NMDA receptor antibodies was not
performed in our patient. However, this entity is most commonly
diagnosed in young women (often with ovarian teratoma), and a
number of core clinical features, including the electrophysiological
abnormalities, the cranial nerve/brain stem signs as well as the long
tract signs, cannot be explained by this differential diagnosis. The key
diagnostic feature was the continuous motor unit activity on EMG in
axial muscles, which is pathognomonic for SPS and PERM.
Of note, most of the features, which have been described to reliably
differentiate PERM from SPS, were present in our patient, including
oculomotor signs, positive Babinski sign, ataxia and epileptic seizures.
The fact that no GADab were detected is not unusual: up to one
quarter of PERM patients do not have antibodies against GAD [2].
A causal relationship between the neurological syndrome and HL
is evident, especially since polychemotherapy of HL resulted in
prompt and sustained improvement of all neurological signs and
symptoms. An association of PERM and SPS with solid tumors and,
more rarely, with hematologic malignancies is well established,
although the precise mechanisms are not completely understood. In
particular, three cases of SPS in the setting of HL have been reported,

with diverse patterns of temporal relationship between SPS and HL:
Ferrari and colleagues described a patient with established HL, in
whom a relapse of HL was accompanied by SPS [5]. Gutmann et al.
reported a 55-year-old woman in whom SPS preceded diagnosis of
HL by 14 months [6]. Finally, Werbrouck et al. presented a man in
whom SPS occurred after remission of HL [7]. In two of these cases
[6,7], SPS was accompanied by other presumably paraneoplastic
manifestations.
Against this background, our case deserves particular attention,
since it shows that PERM can also occur in the setting of HL. As
described by Gutmann et al., the neurological symptoms did precede
the diagnosis of HL by several months. At the time of onset of PERM,
extensive systemic investigations including PET-CT and biopsy
showed no signs of malignancy. However, we cannot exclude with
complete certainty the possibility that HL may have been present at
this time. Possible failure to identify HL might be explained by a
ﬂuctuating course of the malignant disease in its initial stages [10];
another explanation is that the long-term corticosteroid treatment
may have initially masked or controlled the lymphoma. Interestingly,
and in contrast to Gutmann et al. [6], in our patient the diagnosis of HL
was
established during an elective follow-up evaluation, i.e. in the
absence of other clinical manifestations of HL such as dyspnea, pleural
effusion or other symptoms.
In conclusion, we here show that not only SPS, but also PERM can
be associated with HL. Our case highlights the clinical lesson that
patients with probable SPS or PERM require early, rigorous and
frequent follow-up investigations to detect otherwise clinically
asymptomatic malignancies including HL, especially if initial work-
up during the onset of neurological symptoms is unremarkable.
